reviews, see O’Fallon & Butterﬁeld, 2005; Tenbrunsel & Smith-Crowe,

illustrated that both characteristics of the individual actors

Researchers examining situational factors have shown that uneth-
ical behavior is more likely to occur in egoistic ethical climates

Table 3 presents the results obtained for the originality of leadership plans in the analysis of covariance. Openness proved to be a

that category and were all part of the high scorers group (59.6% of that group). Finally, we
had 24.9% of the high scorers sample (N ¼ 13) above or equal to the clinical threshold

We used a paradigm in which
participants committed a transgression against another
participant (Leunissen et al., 2012; Desmet & Leunissen,
2014). This paradigm is based on a trust game (Berg,
Dickhaut, & McCabe, 1995). In the original version of the
trust game, Player 1 starts with an initial endowment (i.e.,
chips) and has the choice to transfer any part of this
endowment to Player 2. Whatever Player 1 transfers to
Player 2 is tripled. Player 2 can then decide to return any
part of his/her endowment to Player 1. In a trust game,
participants often base their behaviour on the equality
fairness rule, meaning that both players should end up with
an equal share of the chips (Van Dijk & De Cremer, 2006).
Keeping a larger share is considered unfair behaviour and
constitutes a transgression.
In this modiﬁed version of the trust game, participants
always took the role of Player 2 (assigned through a mock
lottery procedure) and played with a ﬁctitious Player 1.
Participants did not know the exact size of Player 1’s initial
endowment; they only knew that it could range from 10 to
30 chips. Player 2 subsequently learned that Player 1 had
transferred 10 chips, which were tripled, endowing Player 2
with 30 chips. We expected that most participants would
infer that Player 1 had an initial endowment larger than 10
chips, because 10 was at the very low end of the range of
possible endowments with which Player 1 could have
started. Consequently, most participants would feel justiﬁed

5.1.3. Manipulations
5.1.3.1. Task A regulatory focus. The regulatory focus of Task A was
manipulated by modifying Task A framing in a manner consistent
with prior research (Freitas et al., 2002; Shah, Higgins, & Friedman,
1998). For those assigned to the promotion frame, Task A was

unique words.” This framing was reinforced when participants
were interrupted, with the experimenter telling them: ‘‘At this
point, I need to interrupt you on this task [. . .]. But I will give
you 5 more minutes at the end of the experiment for you to try
to ﬁnish this task and meet the target of answering all 17 clues with
only 5 unique words.”

described as a risk to fail by not completing the task. The task goal
was presented in terms of solutions left unfound. For example, par-

17 clues using only 5 unique words. You will fail to complete the
task if you don’t ﬁnd these 5 unique words.” This framing was also

DISCUSSION
Our findings show that the decrease seen in total
government school enrollments can be almost en-
tirely accounted for by a decrease in students en-
rolled in the mainstream. Whereas mainstream
enrollments as a percentage of total enrollments
decreased between 1997 and 2009, SC Secondary
and SSP enrollments increased. SC Elementary
enrollments fluctuated across the time period of
interest, thus resulting in an overall flat trend.

Confirmatory factor analysis
We tested our measurement model using CFA in MPlus version 7
(Muthén & Muthén, 1998–2012). For the indicators of the organiza-
tional identity latent variable, we formed three parcels on the basis
of the subscales of this measure, which is a recommended step given
that these item sets should share secondary covariance that would
otherwise distort the results of the CFA (Hall, Snell, & Foust, 1999).
Following best practices for parceling (Williams & O’Boyle, 2008), we
evaluated the reliability of each parcel. Specifically, the three parcels
consisted of the means of the three solidarity items (α = .91), the three
identity centrality items (α = .88), and the four identity satisfaction
items (α = .92). Because the constructive deviance and normative
conflict measures are not multidimensional, we used the individual
items as the indicators for their respective latent variables.

Willingness to Be Interrupted Now.
A logistic regression
analysis showed that more people chose to play the 5-minute
iPad game now when they were far from the goal rather

goal completion. We found no differences in spare time

to these ﬁndings in “Meta-Analysis of Results of Studies 1
through 4.”

Leader development
A review of more than a century's studies on psychological aspects of leadership reveals a notable absence of comprehensive and
methodical discussion and research on developmental psychological aspects of leaders (Avolio, 1999, 2005; Avolio & Gibbons, 1988;
Day, Zaccaro, & Halpin, 2004; Klonsky,1983; Kuhnert & Lewis,1987; London, 2002; McCauley, & Van Velsor, 2004; Popper & Mayseless,
2002; Zacharatos, Barling, & Kelloway, 2000).
Most evidence on the development of leaders has been supplied by historians who studied the lives of outstanding leaders (e.g.,
Bullock,1991; Burns,1956). Characteristically, these studies (1) focus on exceptional leaders who are of great interest to historians, and
(2) analyze their development mainly from a psychoanalytic viewpoint (Burns, 1978). Such studies are clearly limited with regard to
the possibility of generalization. This criticism is often directed at psychoanalytical research in general (Meadow, 1996), but it is even
more relevant in the case of historical studies of outstanding (usually political) personages (Burns,1978). They do not necessarily shed
light on leaders of local communities, organizational units, social frameworks, and the like, namely those who might be described as
“leaders in everyday life.”
A more comprehensive analysis of leaders' development is to be found in the works of scholars who discuss psychological

Conscientiousness.
Conscientiousness was assessed using
the Conscientiousness subscale of the Big Five Personality Inven-
tory—Short (Goldberg, 1999). This measure requires individuals
to report agreement with 10 items that assess conscientiousness

Internal consistency was high. (Coefficient alpha was .81 for men
and .85 for women.)
